name: Hermeticism
era: 1st to 3rd century CE, revived from the 15th century
line: Look for the pattern, watch the mind and work the slow stages.

quote.text: That which is below is like that which is above, and that which is above is like that which is below, to do the miracles of one only thing.
quote.source: Tabula Smaragdina, trans. after Isaac Newton’s manuscript version

quotes.text: A great wonder, Asclepius, is the human being.
quotes.source: Hermetic dialogue, Latin text, 3rd to 4th century CE

quotes.text: Unless you make yourself equal to God, you cannot understand God; like is understood by like.
quotes.source: Corpus Hermeticum XI, trans. after Brian Copenhaver

quotes.text: All things are poison and nothing is without poison; only the dose makes a thing not a poison.

words.meaning: Hermes the Thrice-Greatest; the legendary author of the Hermetica
words.usage: A figure who joined the Greek Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth, honoured as a teacher of wisdom.

words.meaning: The writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus
words.usage: Philosophical dialogues and technical texts on astrology, alchemy and magic from the first centuries CE.

words.meaning: The collection of seventeen Greek Hermetic treatises
words.usage: Copied in Byzantium and translated into Latin by Ficino in 1463.

words.meaning: The first treatise of the Corpus; often read as "shepherd of men"
words.usage: A vision in which Mind reveals the origin of the cosmos and the soul’s ascent.

words.meaning: A Hermetic dialogue surviving in Latin
words.usage: Known in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, with its famous praise of the human being.
In the Hermetica it is both a god and the divine part of a person.
The organising word or reason that shapes the cosmos.
In the Hermetica, knowledge of God and the self, rather than information.
The root of "cosmetic". The world seen as an ordered, beautiful whole.

words.meaning: The small world; a human being
words.usage: The idea that a person mirrors the larger cosmos.
The cosmos regarded as a living whole in which a person is a part.

words.meaning: The link between things at different levels
words.usage: The thought that a pattern repeats across scales.

words.meaning: First matter; the raw stuff of the work
words.usage: In alchemy, the basic material from which everything is made, and what the work begins with.
The long process of transformation. In alchemy it was the making of the philosophers’ stone.
The stage of dissolution and darkness.
The stage of washing and clarification.
A stage that was later often dropped from the sequence of colours.
The stage of completion.
From the Arabic at-tannur, an oven that burns steadily.
From the Arabic al-anbiq, which came from a Greek word for a cup.
From the Arabic al-iksir, a powder or agent that perfects.
The fifth element, beyond earth, water, air and fire.

words.meaning: The serpent that bites its own tail
words.usage: A symbol of cycle and unity, found in Greco-Egyptian alchemical texts.
The idea that the cosmos is a living being.
An alchemical motto for the repeated cycle of breaking down and making whole.
A short, cryptic text from the Arabic tradition, famed for the line "as above, so below".

words.meaning: God-working; ritual union with the divine
words.usage: A practice of late antique philosophers. Not part of this Onda.
The subject of Corpus Hermeticum XIII, in which a student is "born again" in mind.

words.meaning: Fate; the rule of the stars
words.usage: The compulsion of planetary powers from which the Hermetic teaching promises release.
The idea that the parts of the cosmos influence each other.

words.meaning: A Paracelsian art of separating and recombining
words.usage: Coined by Paracelsus from words for "to separate" and "to join".

words.meaning: The Roman Mercury; the spirit of change in alchemy
words.usage: Alchemy used the name for both the planet, the metal and a restless, shape-changing principle.
A modern text, not an ancient one. Its seven principles come from it.

practices.name: A page at dawn
practices.instructions: Read one short passage from a Hermetic text in a reliable translation, such as the opening vision of the Poimandres, in no more than a page. Read it slowly twice. Then close the book and sit for five minutes with one line in mind. Ask what it would mean if it were literally true and what it would mean as a figure of speech. Write a sentence.
practices.why: The Hermetic writings present themselves as teaching through vision and dialogue rather than argument. A short, slow reading each morning treats them as that: something to be seen as much as understood.
variations: Read the same page three days in a row.
Copy the passage by hand.
Read it aloud to someone and ask what they hear.

practices.name: Watching the mind
practices.instructions: Sit upright. Set a timer for ten minutes. Close your eyes or lower your gaze. Notice thoughts as they appear, as if you were watching them pass on a screen. Label them lightly: planning, remembering, worrying. Do not follow them or push them away. When you notice you have been carried off, return to watching. At the end ask: who was watching?
practices.why: In the Hermetic texts Mind, nous, is both a divine reality and the highest part of a person, and knowing oneself leads to knowing the whole. A simple watching of the mind is a modest way in.
variations: Do it outdoors with your eyes open.
Count breaths from one to ten and begin again.
Write down the most frequent type of thought.

practices.name: Name today’s planet
practices.instructions: Look at the day of the week and name its planet: Sunday the Sun, Monday the Moon, Tuesday Mars, Wednesday Mercury, Thursday Jupiter, Friday Venus, Saturday Saturn. English weekdays and the Romance languages still carry the old planetary order. Spend a minute with its quality: Mars for effort, Mercury for talk, Venus for pleasure. Treat it as a symbol, a way of colouring the day.
practices.why: The planetary week came from Hellenistic Egypt and is still in our calendar. Whatever you think of astrology, it is a curious pleasure to live in a week named for the wandering stars.
variations: Find which language keeps the planet most clearly.
Wear a colour for the planet.
Look up where the planet is in the sky tonight.

practices.name: A laboratory page
practices.instructions: Open a notebook and write one entry like an early chemist: the date, what you observed, what you did, what happened. Choose one small experiment, such as I will not check my phone until ten, and record the result. Be exact, and leave out opinions. Early alchemists and chemists kept notebooks, and so did Newton, who kept a great many.
practices.why: The rule of this Onda is to write down what you see. A habit of dated observation is the common root of alchemy, chemistry and good thinking.
variations: Record the weather at the same hour each day.
Record one dream as a field note.
Record the result of a kitchen experiment.

practices.name: Test one claim
practices.instructions: Pick one claim you have been told, or have told yourself, and test it. Look for the source. Ask what would show it false. Spend ten minutes on it. The first rule of this Onda is to test what you are told. Hermetic writings invite the reader to see for themselves, and a good reader asks for evidence before belief.
practices.why: The Hermetic tradition and early science grew up side by side. Testing a claim before accepting it is the best habit either tradition gave us.
variations: Test a claim from a trusted friend.
Test one from the news.
Test one from yourself: Am I really always late?

practices.name: Draw the ouroboros
practices.instructions: Draw the serpent that bites its own tail, the ouroboros, in a few strokes. Make it simple, a circle with a head and a tail, and then add one thing inside it that, for you, goes round and round: a habit, a season, a quarrel. Look at it. The symbol is Egyptian, taken into Greek and alchemical thought as a picture of the whole that is one.
practices.why: The ouroboros appears in Egyptian and Hellenistic sources and in alchemical manuscripts as an emblem of unity and cycle. Drawing it is a good way to think about what comes back.
variations: Draw it with the words one is all around the edge.
Draw it in clay.
Find five ouroboroi in pictures online.

practices.name: As above, so below
practices.instructions: Find one pattern that repeats at two scales: the branching of a river and of a tree, a spiral in a shell and in a galaxy picture, the rhythm of your breath and of the day. Look at both for a few minutes and draw the shared form. Then ask whether something in your own life repeats at a small and a large scale: a habit and a pattern.
practices.why: The Emerald Tablet’s famous line says that what is below is like what is above. Whatever the truth of cosmic claims, looking for the same pattern at different sizes is a good habit of attention.
variations: Look at a leaf with a magnifying glass and then at a satellite map.
Draw the pattern and give it a name.
Share the correspondence with a friend.

practices.name: One line of the Emerald Tablet
practices.instructions: Read one line of the Emerald Tablet in a translation you trust. Copy it out by hand. Write what it could mean in an ordinary day, then what it could mean at a larger scale (a city, the sky, a life). Note any doubt or disagreement without hurrying to resolve it.
practices.why: The Emerald Tablet is a short, famously obscure text that shaped centuries of alchemy and natural philosophy. Slow reading is the right speed for it.
variations: Read it aloud.
Compare two translations.
Draw the line as a diagram.

practices.name: Walk and notice patterns
practices.instructions: Take a short walk and look for patterns: spirals, branches, waves, hexagons, rhythms of spacing. Notice them in a hedge, a puddle, a fence, the clouds. Point out three to yourself. The correspondence practice made physical: the world is full of the same few shapes, repeated. When you get back, draw your favourite.
practices.why: Hermetic writers saw the cosmos as a web of correspondences. A walk that looks for repeated patterns is a gentle, modern version of that way of seeing.
variations: Take a camera and collect patterns.
Walk with a child and let them find them.
Walk by water.

practices.name: Microcosm and macrocosm
practices.instructions: Write three parallels between your body and the world: the heartbeat and the tide, the breath and the wind, the blood and the river. Pick one and sit with it for a minute. The human being, said the Hermetic writers, is a small world, a microcosm, mirroring the great one, the macrocosm. Treat it as a poem, and see what it shows.
practices.why: The doctrine of the microcosm and the macrocosm was central to Renaissance Hermeticism, in Ficino and Paracelsus. A list of parallels is a good thought experiment, whatever you believe.
variations: Add the seasons of life and the year.
Draw the body as a map of the world.
Share your list with someone.

practices.name: Name the stage
practices.instructions: Choose a project or a situation and name which alchemical stage it is in: nigredo, the blackening, where things break down; albedo, the whitening, where they clear; citrinitas, the yellowing, the dawn; rubedo, the reddening, the final stage. Write one sentence on what that stage asks. Work slowly, in stages.
practices.why: The alchemists described the Great Work in colour stages. As a metaphor for any slow change, it gives a useful vocabulary for where you are, and a reason to be patient.
variations: Name the stage of a friendship.
Name the stage of your day.
Name the stage of a recipe or craft you are making.

practices.name: An hour of silence
practices.instructions: Spend an hour without talking and without media: no podcast, no music, no news. Do your usual tasks, or take a walk. Notice how often you want to fill the silence. The Hermetic texts speak of silence as the condition of insight, and they teach that the deepest things are not said easily. Keep your own counsel for an hour.
practices.why: This Onda’s fourth rule is to keep your own counsel. The Hermetic writings tell of mysteries told in silence. An hour without talk is a practical way of finding out what you think.
variations: Do it on a walk.
Do it on a morning at home.
Break it by writing, not speaking.

practices.name: Solve et coagula
practices.instructions: Choose one problem or confusion that is on your mind. First dissolve it: write down every part, doubt, fear and fact on a page, without ordering them. Leave it for a minute. Then bring it together: write a single sentence, or a short list, that says what the problem really is and the next small step. Name the stage you are in: blackening, whitening, yellowing, reddening.
practices.why: Alchemists described the work as a cycle of breaking down and making whole, passing through colour stages. Used as a metaphor for thinking and change, it is a sound method.
variations: Use it on a conflict with another person.
Use it on a piece of writing.
Keep a record of which stage you were in each night.

practices.name: Sky log
practices.instructions: Go out and look at the sky, and write a line in a log: the date, the time, the Moon’s phase, any planet you can see, the weather. Over days, you will see the Moon change and the planets walk. The old Hermetic world was built on watching the sky, and keeping a log is the simplest and most scientific way to join it.
practices.why: Hermetic and alchemical writers drew on astronomy and astrology, and kept careful logs. A sky log is a pleasure in itself, and over a month it shows you the pattern of the heavens.
variations: Add the temperature.
Mark where the Moon rises.
Go out at the same time each night.

practices.name: Read an emblem
practices.instructions: Look at one emblem from Michael Maier’s Atalanta Fugiens or another alchemical emblem book: a picture, a verse and a motto. Look at the picture for a full minute, then read the verse, then decide what the emblem is saying. Write a sentence. Emblems are puzzles for the eye and the mind, and meant to be read slowly.
practices.why: Atalanta Fugiens, from 1617, offers fifty emblems with verses and fugues on the stages of the Work. They are among the most beautiful and strange pictures of the period.
variations: Read three in one evening.
Make an emblem of your own: a drawing, a line and a motto.
Read one aloud to someone.

practices.name: What I will not say
practices.instructions: Write down one thing you are not going to say to anyone, and why. It might be a secret, a hope, a judgment. You do not have to burn it or publish it. Just see it. The fourth rule of this Onda is to keep your own counsel, and it begins by knowing what you are keeping. Read it, then leave it on the page.
practices.why: Hermetic writings and alchemical texts are full of secrets and silence. Whatever the reason, a habit of deciding what to keep private is an old and useful discipline.
variations: Write what you will say tomorrow instead.
Write what you wish you could say.
Write why it is yours to keep.

practices.name: Fill a magic square
practices.instructions: Draw a three-by-three square and fill it with the numbers one to nine so that every row, column and diagonal adds up to fifteen. It is the square of Saturn in the old planetary scheme, and Dürer put a larger one in his engraving Melencolia I. Work slowly. Look up the answer only at the end. It is a pleasure like a crossword.
practices.why: Magic squares belonged to the planetary lore of the Hermetic tradition: each planet had its own. They are also pure mathematical fun, and a quiet way to end an evening.
variations: Try the four-by-four square from Dürer.
Make a square for a friend.
Time yourself and try again tomorrow.

practices.name: A dialogue with your nous
practices.instructions: The Poimandres is a dialogue between a seeker and a vast Mind. Write a short dialogue between you and your own Mind: you ask a real question, and let an answer come. Write fast, without editing, for ten minutes. Do not claim it as revelation. See what the voice has to say, and notice how it differs from your usual one.
practices.why: The Hermetic texts are often dialogues, with a teacher and a pupil, or a human and a divine Mind. A written dialogue is a safe, old way to think a question through.
variations: Ask the question aloud first.
Let the Mind be a wise person you know.
Write the answer with your other hand.

practices.name: A night watch
practices.instructions: On a clear night, go outside and watch the sky turn. Note where a bright star or planet is at the start, against a roof or tree. Come back after twenty and forty minutes and see how far it has moved. You are watching the Earth turn. The ancients thought the stars were writing, and learned to read it. Bring a hot drink.
practices.why: Watching the sky for a long stretch is the best way to feel its motion. The Hermetic and astronomical traditions began with this simple act, repeated over generations.
variations: Use a free sky app to name what you see.
Do it with a friend.
Do it again the same night next week.

practices.name: The Work in a kitchen
practices.instructions: Make something in stages, as an alchemist would: jam, bread, a slow stew, a batch of biscuits. Name each stage by colour as it goes: the dark of raw things, the whitening, the golden browning, the final red. Take your time and notice the changes. Do not taste anything unknown or heat anything strange. Eat and share the result.
practices.why: Alchemical language of stages and colour describes real changes of matter, and also a way of working with patience. Cooking is its everyday, safe cousin.
variations: Make bread.
Make a batch of jam.
Make a stew that takes three hours.

immersePlan.name: Read the opening of the Poimandres
immersePlan.text: Open Copenhaver’s translation of the Hermetica and read the opening vision of the Poimandres, in which a vast Mind speaks to the seeker. Read it slowly, aloud if you can.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of The Secrets of Alchemy
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Lawrence Principe’s book, by a historian who is also a chemist, on what alchemy really was. Notice how much of it was careful laboratory work.

immersePlan.name: Read about the Hermetic writings in their time
immersePlan.text: Read the opening chapter of Garth Fowden’s study of the Hermetic writings in their late antique setting. Notice who read them, and why.

immersePlan.name: Watch Newton’s Dark Secrets
immersePlan.text: Watch the NOVA documentary on Newton’s alchemical and theological interests. Notice how the founder of modern physics kept notebooks of alchemy.

immersePlan.name: Watch Prospero’s Books
immersePlan.text: Watch Peter Greenaway’s visual feast based on The Tempest, whose hero is a Renaissance magus. Enjoy the books, the colours and the strangeness. Do not try to follow every image.

immersePlan.name: Watch Agora
immersePlan.text: Watch the film set in late antique Alexandria, where Hermetic and Neoplatonic writings were read, with the philosopher Hypatia as its heroine. A historical drama with liberties. Enjoy the city and its debates.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Holst’s The Planets
immersePlan.text: Play Holst’s suite, in which each movement is named for a planet and its astrological character. Listen to Mars first, then Venus, and notice how they colour the mind.

immersePlan.name: Listen to an aria from The Magic Flute
immersePlan.text: Play a few numbers from Mozart’s opera, in which Masonic and Egyptian imagery and ideas of initiation are mixed with fairy tale. Notice how light and shadow are used.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Maier’s fugues
immersePlan.text: Play a modern recording of one of the fugues from Michael Maier’s emblem book of 1617. Look at the emblem that goes with it while it plays.

immersePlan.name: Look at an emblem of Atalanta Fugiens
immersePlan.text: Look at one of the fifty engraved emblems, by Matthaeus Merian for Michael Maier, on the stages of the Work. Look for a minute before you read the verse.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Splendor Solis
immersePlan.text: Look at pages of the richly painted German manuscript of about 1532, now in the British Library. Find the page that shows the bath, and the one that shows the sun.

immersePlan.name: Look at Dürer’s Melencolia I
immersePlan.text: Look at the engraving of a brooding angel among tools and a magic square. Find the square, the scales, the sleeping dog and the compasses. Ask what the angel is thinking.

immersePlan.name: Eat lentils and bread
immersePlan.text: Cook a pot of lentils with onion and olive oil and eat it with bread. It is the everyday food of the Egypt in which the Hermetic writings were composed. Read a page while you eat.

immersePlan.name: Eat figs and dates
immersePlan.text: Eat a few figs and dates slowly, with water. Sit down with a book and enjoy a simple sweet, as a Renaissance scholar might.

immersePlan.name: Eat bread, honey and cheese
immersePlan.text: Slice bread, spread a little cheese and drizzle honey over it. Eat slowly. Honey was the ancient world’s sweetener and a plain pleasure.

immersePlan.name: Make barley water
immersePlan.text: Boil a handful of pearl barley in water, cool, strain and add lemon if you like. It is the old Greek ptisane. Drink it slowly in the evening.

immersePlan.name: Mix wine and water as the Greeks did
immersePlan.text: If you drink wine, mix one part with two or three of water and sip it. If not, mix grape juice and water. Say what you are grateful for.

immersePlan.name: Brew sage tea
immersePlan.text: Steep a few fresh sage leaves in hot water for five minutes. Only use herbs you know are safe. Sage was prized in medieval and Renaissance herbals. Drink slowly.

immersePlan.name: Keep a laboratory notebook
immersePlan.text: Write the date, what you observed, what you did and what happened, as an early chemist would. Choose a small thing to observe and record it.

immersePlan.name: Walk and notice patterns
immersePlan.text: Take a short walk in nature with attention to patterns: spirals, branches, waves. Name three of them. It is the correspondence practice made physical.

immersePlan.name: Name the planet of the day
immersePlan.text: English weekdays still carry the old planetary order. Treat each day as a symbol: Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn. Say today’s planet and what it might colour.

immersePlan.name: Play a hand of tarocchi or look at the trumps
immersePlan.text: The painted trumps began as a card game for the courts of Milan and Ferrara in the fifteenth century. Look at a set of trumps and pick the one you like most. Do not use them to tell the future; read them as pictures.

immersePlan.name: Play Opus Magnum
immersePlan.text: If you have the puzzle game by Zachtronics, build a small machine that transmutes elements. If not, draw a diagram of how you would turn lead to gold with gears.

immersePlan.name: Play Alchemists
immersePlan.text: Play the board game in which you mix ingredients, test the result and publish theories. If you cannot, read the rules and imagine a round. Notice what the game says about doing science.

immersePlan.name: Mark the equinox
immersePlan.text: Hermetic orders since the nineteenth century have marked the two days of the year when day and night are equal. Find out when the next is, and on that day sit outdoors at noon and note the length of your shadow.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Siena pavement of Hermes
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the 1488 marble panel just inside the main door of Siena Cathedral, showing Hermes Trismegistus. Notice that a pagan sage was honoured at the door of a church.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Ritman library
immersePlan.text: Look up the library of Hermetic, alchemical and Rosicrucian books in Amsterdam. Browse its online collection and find one title that you would like to read.

immersePlan.name: Find one correspondence
immersePlan.text: Correspondence is the link between things at different scales. Find one today, and say it aloud: this is like that. Write it in one line.

immersePlan.name: Say solve et coagula
immersePlan.text: Solve et coagula, dissolve and bring together. Choose something that needs to be broken down and then built up again, a plan, a paragraph, a room, and do it in two steps.

immersePlan.name: Think of an ouroboros in your life
immersePlan.text: The ouroboros is the serpent that bites its own tail. Name one thing in your life that goes round: a habit, a season, a worry. Draw it as a circle and add one arrow where you might break or bless the cycle.

rules.why: Renaissance and early modern alchemists were also experimenters. Check your claims against what you can observe.
Alchemical and scientific notebooks record observations. A record turns an impression into evidence.

rules.text: Look for the pattern beneath the surface
rules.why: The Hermetic habit is to ask what links things. Start with what repeats.
The word “hermetic” came to mean sealed and secret. Practise discretion: not everything you learn needs sharing.
The Great Work is long. Do not hurry the change you want, and notice which stage you are in.

rules.text: Never ingest or heat unknown substances
rules.why: This Onda uses alchemy as a symbol only. Mercury, arsenic and many old alchemical materials are poisons.

read.why: The standard modern English translation, with notes.

read.why: A smaller translation of the Corpus Hermeticum and the Definitions of Hermes to Asclepius.

read.creator: Garth Fowden
read.why: A historical study of the Hermetic writings in their late antique setting.

read.title: The Secrets of Alchemy
read.creator: Lawrence M. Principe
read.why: A historian and chemist on what alchemy really was.

read.title: Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition
read.creator: Frances A. Yates
read.why: An influential and much debated study of Renaissance Hermeticism.

read.title: Hermetic Spirituality and the Historical Imagination
read.creator: Wouter J. Hanegraaff
read.why: A careful modern study of how the Hermetic texts were read.

read.title: The Kybalion
read.creator: Three Initiates
read.why: A modern book that presents seven "Hermetic principles". It is not an ancient text and should be read as such.

watch.title: Newton’s Dark Secrets
watch.creator: NOVA, PBS
watch.why: A documentary on Newton’s alchemical and theological interests.

watch.title: Prospero’s Books
watch.creator: Peter Greenaway
watch.why: A visual feast based on The Tempest, whose hero is a Renaissance magus with a library of imagined books.

watch.title: Agora
watch.creator: Alejandro Amenábar
watch.why: A film set in late antique Alexandria, where Hermetic and Neoplatonic writings were read, with the philosopher Hypatia as its heroine. A historical drama with liberties; enjoy the city.

listen.title: The Planets
listen.creator: Gustav Holst
listen.why: A suite for orchestra, each movement named for a planet and its astrological character.

listen.title: The Magic Flute
listen.creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
listen.why: An opera in which Masonic and Egyptian imagery, and ideas of initiation and light, are woven into the story.

listen.title: Atalanta Fugiens: fugues for three voices
listen.creator: Michael Maier
listen.why: Maier’s emblem book contains fifty musical fugues. Modern recordings exist.

art.title: Atalanta Fugiens
art.creator: Michael Maier, engravings by Matthaeus Merian
art.why: Fifty emblems with verses and fugues on the stages of the Work.

art.title: Splendor Solis
art.creator: Anonymous, manuscript
art.why: A richly painted German manuscript, now in the British Library.

art.title: Melencolia I
art.creator: Albrecht Dürer
art.why: An engraving of a brooding angel among tools and a magic square.

art.title: The Siena Cathedral pavement of Hermes Trismegistus
art.creator: Giovanni di Stefano
art.why: A marble inlay in the cathedral floor showing "Hermes Mercurius Contemporaneus Moses".

eat.title: Lentils and bread
eat.creator: Plain fare of Hellenistic Egypt
eat.why: The everyday food of the Greek-speaking Egypt in which the Hermetic writings were composed. Eat it slowly, as a reader of old books might.

eat.title: Figs and dates
eat.creator: Fruit of the eastern Mediterranean
eat.why: Sweet fruits eaten fresh and dried in the ancient and Renaissance Mediterranean. A plain pleasure to eat while you read.

eat.title: Bread, honey and cheese
eat.creator: A simple snack of the Hellenistic world
eat.why: Honey was the ancient world’s sweetener. A snack in the spirit of the age, eaten slowly with a good book.

drink.title: Barley water
drink.creator: Greek ptisane
drink.why: A plain drink of boiled barley, cooled and strained, known to the Greeks as ptisane. A gentle, non-alcoholic drink for a quiet evening of reading.

drink.title: Wine mixed with water
drink.creator: Greek and Egyptian custom
drink.why: In the Hellenistic world wine was drunk mixed with water. Non-drinkers can mix grape juice and water and drink it the same way.

drink.title: Sage tea
drink.creator: A herb of old herbals
drink.why: Sage was prized in medieval and Renaissance herbals. A cup of tea of fresh leaves is a pleasant way to end the day. Only use herbs you know are safe.

customs.title: Keep a notebook like a laboratory journal
customs.creator: Date, observation, result
customs.why: Early chemists and alchemists kept notebooks. Yours can hold observations, patterns and questions.

customs.title: Walk and notice patterns
customs.creator: A short walk in nature with attention to repeating forms

customs.title: Mark the days of the week as planetary names
customs.creator: Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn
customs.why: English weekdays still carry the old planetary order. Treat it as symbol and history, not prediction.

customs.title: Spend an hour in silence
customs.creator: No talking, no media
customs.why: The Hermetic texts speak of silence as the condition of insight.

games.title: Tarot
games.creator: Card game · Italy
games.why: The painted trumps began as a card game for the courts of Milan and Ferrara. Reading them as a book of hidden wisdom started in France in the 1780s.

games.title: Opus Magnum
games.creator: Video game · Zachtronics

ethics.title: Knowledge as responsibility
ethics.text: In the Hermetica knowledge of the self and the cosmos is meant to change the one who knows. To know is to be obliged.
ethics.practice: Pick one thing you know and ask what it asks of you.

ethics.title: Self-mastery
ethics.text: The Poimandres describes the soul stripping away vices as it rises through the planetary spheres. The ideal is freedom from compulsion.
ethics.practice: Name one compulsion and delay it by ten minutes.

ethics.title: Discretion
ethics.text: The word hermetic means sealed. Teachings were passed carefully, to those prepared to receive them. Speaking less can be a form of respect.
ethics.practice: Keep one thing to yourself today, and notice what changes.

ethics.title: Reverence for nature
ethics.text: The Hermetic cosmos is alive and ordered, and the human being is its keystone. Care for the world follows from seeing it as a whole.
ethics.practice: Spend ten minutes caring for something living.

ethics.title: Honest experiment
ethics.text: Early alchemists, and later chemists, tried and recorded. Their best work depended on patience and honest reporting of failures.
ethics.practice: Record one failure from this week without excuses.

ethics.title: Humility before the whole
ethics.text: Hermetic thought sets a person in a vast web of connection. The one who sees the web cannot remain proud.
ethics.practice: Look at the stars for a few minutes and name your smallest worry.

philosophy.title: Mind and cosmos
philosophy.text: The Poimandres begins with a vision of Mind, who tells the seeker that the light is Mind, the same as the divine, and that the person is made of it. A person can know the whole because they share its nature.
philosophy.practice: Spend a moment aware of the awareness behind your thoughts.

philosophy.title: As above, so below
philosophy.text: The phrase comes from a line of the Emerald Tablet, a short text that came into Latin from Arabic in the Middle Ages. It states that the same pattern runs through every level of reality.
philosophy.practice: Look for one pattern at two scales today.

philosophy.title: The One and the All
philosophy.text: Hermetic texts and their Greek background favour the thought that all things are one, "hen to pan". The many things of the world are expressions of a single source.
philosophy.practice: Choose three unlike things you see today and ask what they share.

philosophy.title: Rebirth
philosophy.text: In Corpus Hermeticum XIII, Hermes teaches his son Tat a rebirth in which the vices are driven out and the powers of God enter. It is described as silent and inward.
philosophy.practice: Name one habit you are leaving behind, and write a line to mark it.

philosophy.title: The great wonder
philosophy.text: The Asclepius says that a human being is a great wonder, honoured and adored, because the person is both a mortal body and a divine mind. Pico della Mirandola quoted it in 1486 in his oration on human dignity.
philosophy.practice: Write down something about a human being that amazes you.

philosophy.title: The stages of the work
philosophy.text: Alchemical writers described a process that passed through colours: blackening, whitening, yellowing and reddening. They are taken as stages of change in matter and in the person.
philosophy.practice: Name the stage of a current project.

philosophy.title: Ascent through the spheres
philosophy.text: The Poimandres describes the soul rising through seven planetary spheres, leaving behind a vice at each, until it reaches the eighth and becomes divine. The picture is of a journey of release from compulsion.
philosophy.practice: List the "spheres" of your day and name one burden you could leave at each.

philosophy.title: A living world
philosophy.text: The idea of the anima mundi, a soul of the world, appears in Plato and in Renaissance Hermeticism. It sees nature as alive, not merely a machine.
philosophy.practice: Greet something non-human with attention, such as a tree.

philosophy.title: Silence
philosophy.text: In Corpus Hermeticum XIII the rebirth happens in silence. Whatever the doctrine, a good deal of understanding comes only in the quiet that follows talk.
philosophy.practice: Sit in silence for five minutes with no purpose.

philosophy.title: The modern seven principles
philosophy.text: The Kybalion, published in 1908, lists seven "Hermetic principles": mentalism, correspondence, vibration, polarity, rhythm, cause and effect, and gender. They are a modern synthesis, linked to New Thought, and not part of ancient Hermeticism.
philosophy.practice: If you meet the seven principles, ask where each one comes from before you accept it.

intro: Hermeticism is a tradition of writings and ideas gathered under the name of Hermes Trismegistus, "Hermes the Thrice-Greatest". The name joins the Greek god Hermes, the messenger and guide of souls, with the Egyptian god Thoth, patron of writing and wisdom. Greek-speaking writers in Egypt in the first centuries of the common era composed dialogues under this name, and later readers believed they were far older.

The core is the Corpus Hermeticum, seventeen Greek treatises, and the Latin Asclepius. They mix philosophy, cosmology and spiritual instruction. In the first, the Poimandres, a divine Mind reveals how the cosmos was made and how the soul, having fallen into matter, can rise back through the planetary spheres. Other treatises teach that the universe is alive and orderly, that a human being is a great wonder because both mortal and divine, and that knowledge of the self leads to knowledge of God. Separate "technical" Hermetica deal with astrology, alchemy and magic.

The texts passed into Arabic, where the Emerald Tablet and a large body of alchemical writing took shape, and into medieval Latin. In 1463 Marsilio Ficino, at the request of Cosimo de’ Medici in Florence, translated the Corpus Hermeticum into Latin from a Greek manuscript newly arrived from Macedonia. It was printed in 1471 and read across Europe. Many Renaissance thinkers, including Pico della Mirandola and Giordano Bruno, treated Hermes as an ancient Egyptian sage.

In 1614 the Swiss scholar Isaac Casaubon showed from the language that the texts were not ancient Egyptian but written in the early centuries CE. The finding changed the story but not the interest. The Hermetica remain important as a record of how people thought about mind, cosmos and the divine in late antiquity, and Hermetic ideas shaped alchemy, Renaissance natural philosophy and later occult movements.

Alchemy was not simply a failed attempt to make gold. Its practitioners were also physicians, metalworkers and philosophers who developed laboratory techniques and wrote about transformation in matter and in the person. Isaac Newton left a very large body of alchemical writing alongside his physics. The language of colours, stages and the Great Work offered a rich set of images for change.

Hermeticism today covers several things that should be kept apart: the ancient Hermetica, the Renaissance revival, historical alchemy, and modern esoteric movements such as the Golden Dawn and the authors of the Kybalion, published in 1908. This Onda draws mainly on the first two and treats alchemy as symbol and history. It offers attention, pattern-seeking and a slow method, and does not ask you to practise magic or handle chemicals.

figures.name: Hermes Trismegistus
figures.bio: The name under which the Hermetic texts were written. A blend of the Greek Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth, honoured as a teacher in late antiquity and the Renaissance.

figures.name: Zosimos of Panopolis
figures.bio: A Greco-Egyptian alchemist and writer whose visions and technical works survive in fragments.

figures.name: Jabir ibn Hayyan
figures.bio: A name attached to a large Arabic corpus on alchemy. Scholars debate whether one person wrote it and who he was.

figures.name: Marsilio Ficino
figures.bio: Florentine philosopher who translated the Hermetica and Plato for Cosimo de’ Medici and shaped Renaissance Platonism.

figures.name: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
figures.bio: Italian humanist whose Oration on the Dignity of Man, 1486, drew on the Hermetic praise of the human being.

figures.name: Paracelsus
figures.bio: Swiss physician and alchemist who sought chemical medicines and challenged the authority of ancient writers.

figures.name: John Dee
figures.bio: English mathematician, adviser to Elizabeth I and collector of books, who also pursued alchemy and angelic communication.

figures.name: Giordano Bruno
figures.bio: Italian philosopher who defended an infinite universe and was burned by the Roman Inquisition in 1600.

figures.name: Isaac Casaubon
figures.bio: Classical scholar who dated the Hermetica to the early centuries CE.

figures.name: Michael Maier
figures.bio: German physician and alchemist, author of Atalanta Fugiens.

figures.name: Isaac Newton
figures.bio: Mathematician and physicist who also wrote and collected a huge amount on alchemy and theology.

figures.name: Frances Yates
figures.bio: English historian whose book on Bruno and the Hermetic tradition, 1964, made the subject famous and remains debated.

history.when: c. 3rd century BCE to 2nd century CE
history.detail: In Hellenistic Egypt the Greek Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth were identified. Thoth, the god of writing and wisdom, was honoured at Hermopolis, called by the Greeks the city of Hermes.
Greek-speaking authors in Egypt composed the philosophical Hermetica, such as the Poimandres, and the technical Hermetica on astrology, alchemy and magic.
The alchemist wrote on the preparation of metals and recorded dream-like visions of transformation. He is one of the first named alchemists.
A Latin translation of a Greek Hermetic dialogue was made, and it reached medieval readers. It includes the praise of the human being and a controversial passage on animating statues.
In Baghdad and elsewhere translators rendered Greek works into Arabic, and the Emerald Tablet appeared in Arabic alchemical writings.
Robert of Chester translated an Arabic alchemical work in 1144, one of the first alchemical texts in Latin. The Emerald Tablet entered Latin soon after.
A Greek manuscript of the Corpus Hermeticum reached Florence around 1460. Ficino translated it by 1463, and it was printed in 1471.
Pico della Mirandola wrote his oration on the dignity of man, which quotes the Asclepius on the great wonder of the human being.
Isaac Casaubon showed from the Greek that the Hermetica were written in the early centuries CE and not in ancient Egypt, undermining the claim of great antiquity.
Michael Maier published a book of fifty emblems, verses and fugues on alchemy.
The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn was founded in London. It drew on Hermetic and other sources, and influenced twentieth-century occultism.
A book by "Three Initiates", often attributed to William Walker Atkinson, proposed seven Hermetic principles. It is a modern work.
Among the codices found in Egypt were three Hermetic treatises in Coptic, showing the texts were read in Egypt itself.
Brian Copenhaver’s English translation of the Hermetica made the texts accessible to scholars and general readers.

concepts.detail: In the Hermetica Mind is both a god, the source of the cosmos, and the highest part of a person. Knowing oneself as mind is the doorway to knowing God. It is less about thinking than about awareness.

concepts.text: The same pattern at every level.
concepts.detail: The line comes from the Emerald Tablet and is often used to summarise Hermetic thought. It suggests that a person, a society and the cosmos mirror each other. Used as a method, it asks you to look for structure that repeats.
Hermetic gnosis means knowing the divine and the self, not by inference but by insight. It transforms the knower. Many other late antique movements shared the word.

concepts.text: The person as a small world.
concepts.detail: Renaissance Hermeticism developed the idea that a human being contains the structure of the whole cosmos. Illustrations show the body mapped onto stars and planets. The symbol was used in medicine, art and philosophy.

Alchemists called their work the magnum opus. It involved stages of change in matter, often shown by colours, and the transformation of the practitioner. Later writers read it as a symbol of inner development.

Planets, metals, plants, organs and days of the week were thought to correspond. The system appears in astrology, medicine and magic. Modern readers can treat it as a structured set of symbols, not a set of facts.

concepts.text: The inward birth of the new person.
concepts.detail: Corpus Hermeticum XIII has Hermes initiate his son Tat into a rebirth, in which vices leave and divine powers enter. It is reached in silence and cannot be taught except by example.

concepts.text: A short, cryptic text on the unity of things.
concepts.detail: The Tabula Smaragdina first appears in Arabic works of the eighth or ninth centuries and was translated into Latin in the twelfth. Alchemists treated it as a summary of their art. Its language is deliberately obscure.

concepts.text: Fate, the rule of the planets.
concepts.detail: Many in late antiquity felt bound by the stars. The Hermetic texts promise freedom from this compulsion through knowledge, as the soul ascends and sheds each planetary vice.

concepts.text: The seven principles of the Kybalion.
concepts.detail: The 1908 Kybalion proposed seven principles: mentalism, correspondence, vibration, polarity, rhythm, cause and effect, and gender. They reflect early twentieth-century New Thought, not ancient sources, and many popular claims about "Hermetic law" trace back to this book.

facts.text: The phrase "hermetically sealed" comes from alchemy: vessels were sealed with the "seal of Hermes", an airtight closure.
Ficino was told by Cosimo de’ Medici to translate the Hermetica before Plato, because Cosimo was old and eager to read it.
Isaac Casaubon redated the Hermetic writings in 1614, based on the Greek and the lack of any Egyptian influence in their language.
Atalanta Fugiens, published in 1617, includes fifty musical fugues for three voices alongside its emblems.
The Nag Hammadi library, found in 1945, contained Hermetic treatises in Coptic, including a prayer of thanksgiving.
Newton’s surviving papers include a very large quantity of writing on alchemy, much of it unpublished in his lifetime.
Paracelsus’s line that the dose makes the poison is still quoted in toxicology.

glossary.meaning: The Egyptian god of writing and wisdom, identified with Hermes

The early modern word for chemistry and alchemy together

sensitivity.note: Hermeticism includes ancient philosophy, Renaissance learning, historical alchemy and modern esoteric movements. This Onda draws on the first two and treats alchemy as symbol and history. It offers habits of attention and does not ask you to practise ritual magic or handle chemicals.
requiredCaveats: Do not try to make or ingest any alchemical preparations. Many historical materials, such as mercury and arsenic compounds, are poisonous.
The Hermetica were written in the early centuries CE and not in ancient Egypt. The Kybalion and its seven principles are a modern text from 1908.
Astrological and planetary language here is symbolic and historical. It does not predict anything about your life, and nothing here is medical or financial advice.
